final_answer:
Short answer: it does not matter which office indicts first as far as the Guidelines range goes, because the Guidelines make the two districts' conduct one aggregate. What matters is that ONE office should bring everything, and the office with venue over the larger share of the false claims (the larger loss and more counts) should be the one that does. If the facts are otherwise balanced, either office is fine; a second, later prosecution in the other district adds essentially no prison time.

Reasoning. (1) Offense guideline: health care fraud under 18 U.S.C. 1347 is sentenced under USSG 2B1.1 (fraud). Offense level is driven by loss (plus the 2B1.1(b)(7) enhancement for federal health care offenses involving Government health care programs with loss over $1M/$7M/$20M, and likely 3B1.3 abuse of trust/special skill for a physician). (2) Relevant conduct: for offenses such as fraud that are listed in 3D1.2(d) for grouping, 1B1.3(a)(2) counts all acts that were part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan as the offense of conviction, whether or not charged and regardless of the state or district where they occurred. False claims in Georgia and South Carolina by the same doctor, same type of scheme, will almost certainly qualify, so the loss from BOTH states is counted in whichever case is sentenced first. (3) Grouping: if both districts' counts were in one indictment, they group under 3D1.2(d) into a single group, so there is no multiple-count increase from adding counts, but the aggregated loss yields one high offense level. (4) Separate prosecutions do not stack: if a second district later prosecutes conduct already counted as relevant conduct in the first case, USSG 5G1.3(b) requires the sentence to be concurrent and adjusted for time already served on the first term; so a split indictment cannot produce a materially longer sentence and risks double-counting arguments, inconsistent loss findings, and a lower total if the first judge's findings favor the defendant. (5) Statutory ceiling: each 1347 count carries a 10-year maximum (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death). If the aggregated Guidelines range exceeds the 10-year max of one count, USSG 5G1.2(d) lets the court run counts consecutively up to the Guidelines total, so more counts of conviction means a higher achievable ceiling. A single indictment with many counts therefore maximizes time. (6) Venue: each count must be tried where the offense was committed (Constitution art. III, Sixth Amendment, Fed. R. Crim. P. 18); 18 U.S.C. 3237(a) lets a continuing offense be tried in any district in which it was begun, continued or completed. A 1347 execution of the scheme is generally charged where the claim was submitted or executed. Unless claims from one state were submitted, processed or paid in the other district, one district cannot indict the other state's counts, in which case the practical approach is: the office with the larger loss/most counts indicts first and the Guidelines pull the other state's loss in as relevant conduct, with the second office declining or its sentence running concurrent. The Guidelines are the same in both districts, but circuit law differs (Fourth Circuit for South Carolina, Eleventh Circuit for Southern Georgia), most notably on whether Guidelines commentary (e.g., 'intended loss') is entitled to deference; the Nov. 1, 2024 amendment moved intended loss into the text of 2B1.1, largely reducing that gap, but I did not verify current circuit-specific differences, so if one circuit is materially harsher on loss, enhancement or consecutive-sentence practice, that office would be preferred. Caveat: the question gives no loss figures by state, so the recommendation is conditional: indict in the district with the greater share of the fraud (or the one with venue over all counts).

authorities.title: Relevant Conduct
authorities.proposition: For offenses groupable under 3D1.2(d) such as fraud, all acts that were part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan are considered in the offense level.

authorities.title: Groups of Closely Related Counts
authorities.proposition: Fraud counts under 2B1.1 are grouped, producing a single offense level based on aggregate loss.

authorities.title: Imposition of sentence on defendant subject to undischarged term; multiple counts
authorities.proposition: Sentence for relevant-conduct offense runs concurrently and is adjusted for time served; consecutive stacking up to total punishment when range exceeds a single count's statutory maximum.

authorities.title: Health care fraud
authorities.proposition: Up to 10 years per count; 20 if serious bodily injury; life if death.

authorities.title: Offenses begun in one district and completed in another
authorities.proposition: Continuing offenses may be prosecuted in any district in which begun, continued, or completed.

claims.text: Loss from both states is relevant conduct and counted in whichever district sentences first, so the Guidelines range does not depend on which office indicts.
A later prosecution in the other district would run concurrent/adjusted under 5G1.3(b), so splitting adds little time; one consolidated indictment is best.
The indicting office should be the one with venue over, and the largest share of, the false claims; more counts raise the achievable stacked maximum at 10 years per count.
